**Time Dilation:** It is the phenomenon where a clock moving with a relativistic velocity appears to run slower (i.e., time passes more slowly) when measured by an observer in an inertial frame at rest.

**Derivation:**
Let $S'$ be a frame moving with velocity $v$ along the $x$-axis relative to frame $S$. 
Using the Lorentz time transformation:
$$t' = \frac{t - \frac{vx}{c^2}}{\sqrt{1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}}}$$
For a clock at rest in $S'$ at position $x'$, the time interval measured by a stationary clock in $S'$ is $\Delta t' = t'_2 - t'_1$.
The corresponding time interval measured in $S$ is $\Delta t = t_2 - t_1$:
$$\Delta t = \frac{\Delta t'}{\sqrt{1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}}} = \gamma \Delta t'$$
Since $\sqrt{1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}} < 1$, it follows that $\Delta t > \Delta t'$, meaning the moving clock runs slow.
proTip: Always define proper time ($\Delta t'$ measured in the frame where the clock is at rest) clearly in your derivation.
